Newsflash Newsroom , 29.07.2026, 19:51 Healthcare. Romania’s caretaker government has approved hiring procedures for over 6,850 positions in the public healthcare sector. The decision was made amid all-out strikes in the healthcare system, initiated on Tuesday by the Sanitas Federation in nearly 500 public hospitals across the country. Trade unions are unhappy with the serious staff shortage and with the draft unified salary law, which they claim will reduce the income of healthcare workers. Caretaker prime minister Ilie Bolojan says the strike is based on misinformation related to this bill and promises no incomes will be cut. Defence. The Chamber of Deputies in Bucharest on Wednesday adopted the bill to approve the SAFE loan agreement between the European Union and Romania and worth nearly 17 billion euros of investments in defence and strategic infrastructure. Signed in May, the agreement was passed by the deputies in its original form, without amendments. The bill will next go to the Senate, which will have the final say on the matter. Also on Wednesday, the Chamber of Deputies, acting as the decision-making body, passed a bill providing for a temporary and gradual reduction in the excise duty on diesel fuel. The measure will be in force for three months, but may be further extended. Endorsed by all parliamentary groups, it aims to reduce fuel prices at the pump. Drought. The entire Danube basin is faced with severe drought. In Romania, the water flow is three times lower than the average for this period, and experts say that in early August it will get very close to the all-time low of 1,400 cubic meters per second recorded in 1985. Irrigation restrictions are in force in the area, but water supply to the public is not affected. Due to the extremely low level of the Danube, Unit 1 of the Cernavoda Nuclear Power Plant was shut down as a precaution and disconnected from the national energy system on Tuesday. While the state-owned company Nuclearelectrica said it would also conduct a controlled shutdown of the plant’s Reactor 2 on Thursday. A Danube cruise ship with 186 passengers on board ran aground, with the tourists later taken to the Bulgarian port of Vidin while the ship remained stuck in a sandbar on the Romanian shore. Anthem. Military ceremonies were held on Wednesday in Bucharest and in military units across the country to celebrate the National Anthem Day. In a message on this occasion, president Nicuşor Dan says the anthem has preserved its force as a driver of social cohesion and acts as a common denominator of the Romanian identity, represented by citizens within the borders and by communities in the diaspora. National Anthem Day was proclaimed by law in 1998 and is celebrated every year on July 29. Romania’s anthem, Deşteaptă-te române (Awaken, ye Romanian), written by Anton Pann on lyrics by Andrei Mureşanu, was officially performed for the first time in 1848, in the city of Râmnicu Vâlcea, a landmark in national history to this day. Earthquake. The president of Romania Nicuşor Dan on Wednesday sent a message of compassion for the victims of the earthquake that hit Japan. “Deeply saddened by the loss of lives following the earthquake in Japan. My heartfelt condolences go out to the affected families, and I wish a speedy recovery to the injured. Romania stands by Japan in these difficult times,” the president said in a social media post. At least 13 persons died after a 7.1 earthquake struck southwestern Japan on Tuesday, where authorities are carrying out rescue operations and assessing the extent of the damage caused by collapsed buildings, fires, power outages and transport disruptions. Wildfires. A new unit of 40 Romanian firefighters left for France today to help fight wildfires. This is the third unit in the mission carried out by Romania within the framework of the European Union Civil Protection Mechanism. Romania has extended its participation in the firefighting support mission in France by two weeks. Until mid-August, Romanian firefighters will be ready to step in, at the request of the French authorities, alongside the other European teams taking part in the mission. https://nineoclock.ro/murat-kurum-cop31-.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount COP31 President-Designate Murat Kurum has called on world leaders to dramatically step up climate finance, arguing that investment in climate action should be treated as a strategic security priority on a par with long-term defence spending. Speaking on the first day of the Istanbul Climate Finance Summit , Kurum warned that the global climate finance “chasm” must be closed urgently, as governments and financial institutions seek to turn climate commitments into concrete action ahead of COP31 in Antalya. “The world is redefining what security means,” Kurum said, pointing to the major increase in defence-related investment being undertaken by NATO countries. “NATO countries have embarked on a major transformation that will see defence-related investment rise to as much as 5 per cent of GDP. We expect to see ambition on a similar scale when it comes to climate security.” Istanbul Climate Finance Summit Kurum argued that climate investment should be viewed through the same strategic lens as defence spending. “After all, defence spending is considered an investment made today to protect against the threats of tomorrow. Climate investment must be viewed through precisely the same strategic lens,” he said. He added a stark question : “If we no longer have a safe world to live in, what purpose will all our spending to defend our countries serve?” Istanbul Climate Finance Summit A call for stronger political action Kurum called on governments to demonstrate greater political determination and commit additional resources to the global transition to clean energy. “Today, we issue a clear call to leaders around the world: the time has come to show stronger, bolder and more concrete political will on climate action,” he said. He urged countries to increase investment in clean energy, electrification, resilient cities and green industry , while working together to accelerate the transformation of the global economy. The appeal came as the Istanbul summit brought together private banks, international financial institutions, multilateral development banks, climate funds and other major financial actors. The aim is to identify ways of mobilising significantly more public and private capital for climate action and to strengthen cooperation between governments and the financial sector. Finance at the centre of COP31 Climate finance is emerging as one of the defining issues for COP31, which Türkiye will host in Antalya from 9 to 20 November 2026 . The COP31 Presidency has placed implementation at the centre of its agenda, seeking to move the international climate process beyond commitments and towards measurable results. Kurum said finance would be indispensable to that effort. “COP needs to become a place where we can seize the opportunities of climate action and produce concrete outcomes that address the real challenges people face,” he said. “Finance is essential to this effort. Without finance, there is no implementation.” He described the Istanbul Climate Finance Summit as a dedicated space where financial actors could examine how to support the COP31 Presidency’s priorities, ranging from electrification and waste management to resilient cities and oceans. The summit, he said, should help determine how the financial sector can “catalyze and leverage finance at a far greater scale.” BRIDGE initiative moves towards implementation The Istanbul meeting also saw progress on the Climate Implementation Bridge (BRIDGE) , a flagship initiative of the COP31 Presidency. The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) was announced as BRIDGE’s delivery partner, marking an important step towards putting the initiative into operation. Discussions at the summit have also focused on resilient cities and on scaling up climate finance to support the Presidency’s flagship “35-by-35” electrification target . The broader objective is to build stronger links between climate policy and the institutions capable of financing its implementation. From climate pledges to investment For Türkiye, the emphasis on finance is central to its effort to position COP31 as an “implementation COP” — one focused not only on negotiating new commitments, but on delivering tangible outcomes. The approach comes amid growing international pressure to close the gap between the scale of climate investment required and the resources currently available. The Istanbul summit is therefore being used as a bridge between the financial sector and the political negotiations that will culminate in Antalya. Kurum’s message is that climate action can no longer be treated solely as an environmental issue. It is an investment in economic resilience, national security and the stability of the world in which future generations will live. With COP31 less than three months away, the challenge for governments and financial institutions will be to turn that message into concrete commitments — and, ultimately, into capital flowing towards the projects needed to deliver the global climate transition. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqgm.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The victim was working at the anti-plague institute in the Siberia city of Irkutsk By Vicky Wong Â and Â Gabriela Pomeroy Published 7 October 2026 US President Donald Trump says he has a call set up with Vladimir Putin about the death of a lab worker at a plague research centre in Siberia. Russian officials say they are investigating the death of the 28-year-old employee and have not confirmed that the suspected disease is pneumonic plague. They insist there is no risk of an epidemic. Trump told reporters on Wednesday evening he did not believe it was a bioweapon, adding "we're going to find out soon enough, but we don't think so." "If you listen to them, it's under control," he said, referring to Russian authorities. "We hope it is," he added. Reports emerged on Friday of almost 200 people being placed under observation after the death. Referring to China's initial response to the Covid pandemic, Trump said: "Well, China didn't say much, and Russia is not saying much either. But they do say they have it very much under control." Pneumonic plague is a serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague. Trump said the US was in "deep discussions" with Russia, but the Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said no phone call had been scheduled. The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) has called for more transparency from Russia, and requested further information on the lab tests on the individual who died. "We don't yet have the full picture of this event," Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said, adding that the WHO was also seeking "verification of media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause." Ghebreyesus called on Russia to provide "timely, complete and transparent information" in order to clarify "conflicting reports" and help the WHO assess the potential public health risks. Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Putin's spokesman said Russia's reporting of the death to the WHO was in line with standard practice, and accused the media of reporting "false information". The US has issued a formal diplomatic message to Russia requesting additional information. Peskov told reporters he was not aware of such a request. The lab worker, named in Russian media as Darya Shipilova, had reportedly fallen ill a couple of days earlier. Unconfirmed reports suggested that she had become ill after either breaking a test tube containing the pathogen at the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East where she worked or following a field trip to a region where plague occurs naturally among wild rodents. As the US and the WHO sought more information, the country's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, issued a statement saying "there are no epidemic risks for the population of Irkutsk and the Irkutsk region". It said more than 90% of the people who had been in contact with the victim had "completed medical observation" and "no health disorders associated with infectious pathology were detected". Neighbouring Mongolia's government has ordered "health surveillance" measures on its border with Russia, AFP news agency reported. The country's health ministry said it would "maintain continuous surveillance and monitoring to prevent potential risks". This was a precautionary measure, it said, adding "the current risk level is low." Lithuania's health ministry said it has made preparations to manage any possible case in the country. Laboratory testing is available, patients would be isolated in infectious disease hospitals, contacts would be identified, and the country has the stocks of medicines suitable for treatment, according to Nerija Kaulakien, an adviser at the Ministry of Health's Communications Division, in an interview with ELTA news agency. There was no evidence of "an increased risk of plague" at the moment, she said. In the immediate wake of the laboratory worker's death, Russia's health watchdog had issued a statement saying the woman had died of "pneumonia of an undetermined etiology" and that testing found "no microorganisms related to her professional activities". However, after this announcement, a pro-government federal news outlet deleted five posts mentioning a possible plague case, and authorities in the town of Baikalsk deleted a message advising against travel to Shelekhov because of a possible plague infection. Ongoing speculation into the lab worker's death has sparked a back and forth between Russia and the US, with questions about a possible spread outside of Russia. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US had "measures" available to help Russia if the situation turned out to be more serious than claimed. According to the WHO, pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours - and can be fatal, if not diagnosed and treated early. People can be infected through: infected flea bites contact with bodily fluids or contaminated materials the inhalation of respiratory particles Symptoms include shortness of breath and coughing, often with blood-tainted phlegm. The bacterium that causes the plague, Yersinia pestis, found among rodents such as marmots in the area. It killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death . It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, was founded just over 100 years ago. Photograph: Matt Rourke/AP Buffalo shooting Jury selection begins in hate crimes trial for Buffalo supermarket gunman Trial could see white supremacist who killed 10 people in New York state store get the death penalty Associated Press Tue 13 Oct 2026 08.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Jury selection is set to begin Tuesday in the trial that could see the white supremacist who killed 10 people in a 2022 Buffalo supermarket get the death penalty. The attack is believed to be the deadliest shooting targeting Black people in modern history. Payton Gendron is facing more than two dozen federal hate crime charges – and over a dozen firearms charges. He is already spending life in prison on state murder charges. Families of the victims and survivors differ on whether Gendron should be sentenced to death. His defense team is not going to dispute his guilt and instead focus on arguing that he should be spared execution . “Nothing will change the fact that Payton Gendron will die in prison,” the federal public defender office said in a statement. “At trial, we will offer mitigating evidence about Payton that the jury needs to consider in making its decision. Nothing we say or do is intended to be disrespectful or insensitive to the victims, the survivors, or their loved ones.” Some victims’ family members, however, are not totally against the death penalty. “I’ve never been like out here like, ‘Yay! Go for the death penalty.’ That’s never been me,” said Buffalo common council member Zeneta Everhart, who ran for office over a year after her son, Zaire, survived the shooting. “Ten people died that day in an egregious way and in an awful, terrible, traumatic way.” Her son, now 25, and the two other survivors have had their lives irrevocably altered, she added. Gendron drove more than 200 miles (320 kilometers) from his home in Conklin, a predominantly white and rural town, to Buffalo on 14 May 2022. Then 18, he fired around 60 shots from a semiautomatic rifle at employees and shoppers at the Tops Friendly Markets grocery store on Jefferson Avenue. Video revealed Gendron apologized to a white store worker after shooting him in the leg. He surrendered to police as he exited the supermarket. Investigators found past social media posts and other writings by Gendron dedicated to planning an attack to frighten people who were non-white and non-Christian into leaving the US. He also promoted a baseless “great replacement theory” that people of color will replace white people through higher birth rates and immigration. The victims who were killed were all Black and between ages 32 and 86. Besides Chaney, they included Geraldine Talley, Katherine Massey, Pearl Young, Andre Mackneil, church deacon Heyward Patterson, Ruth Whitfield, Roberta Drury, Margus Morrison and Aaron Salter, a retired Buffalo police officer who was working as a security guard. Beside being one of the deadliest acts of anti-Black violence in modern US history, the 2022 Tops mass murder reflects a grim reality represented in national bias crime statistics. Black people have comprised the “number one numerical target” annually since the FBI began collecting data in 1991, according to hate crime analyst Brian Levin, of the California Association of Human Relations Organizations. The record high was 3,670 anti-Black bias incidents in 1996. According to FBI data released in August, law enforcement agencies reported over 2,800 anti-Black hate crime incidents in 2025, nearly three times the number targeting Latinos. The FBI also reported a 7% decline in hate crime incidents from 2024 to 2025. The Buffalo shooting and the 2015 Charleston, South Carolina, church shooting, in which a white gunman killed nine Black churchgoers, show how online radicalization makes this a terrorism matter as well. “Unfortunately, [Gendron] fits the pattern of young, mostly white males undertaking targeted massacres which are then justified by manifestos, which are also part of a continuing chain that references prior attacks often but seeks to encourage future ones,” Levin said. https://www.dw.com/en/serbian-police-sho.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OlB3 An attack has occurred outside the Israeli Embassy in Belgrade Image: Armin Durgut/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement A knife-wielding assailant attacked a police guard outside the Israeli Embassy in the Serbian capital, Belgrade, overnight to Wednesday, slightly wounding the officer before being shot dead by him, Serbia's interior minister said. Interior Minister Ivica Dacic said the attacker, whom he described as a minor, had been monitored by security agencies as a supporter of the terrorist organization "Islamic State" (IS) . The area around the embassy was secured by police after the attack Image: Serbian Interior Ministry/Handout/REUTERS Israel's Foreign Ministry later confirmed an "attempted terrorist attack" near its embassy in Belgrade, adding that no personnel were injured and the incident was being investigated. What else we know about the Belgrade attack? The attacker was thought to come from the western Serbian town of Sabac and "kept the black flag in support of the 'Islamic State' on his Instagram” account," according to the minister. Dacic said the assailant shouted "Allahu Akbar," or "God is great" in Arabic, during the attack on the guard. According to Dacic, the guard killed the attacker in self-defense. He said police were treating the incident as a terrorist attack, with the terrorism threat level raised to its highest, or "red alert." "This means tighter security checks and an increased police presence at sensitive sites, including infrastructure facilities and places where large crowds gather," he said. The attack came just days after key early parliamentary election in Serbia and one day after Israel held its parliamentary vote , with no clear result yet in sight. Police have raised the terror alert to its highest level Image: Serbian Interior Ministry/Handout/REUTERS Previous Israeli Embassy attack in Belgrade In June 2024, an attacker with a crossbow seriously wounded a Serbian police officer guarding the same embassy in Belgrade before being shot and killed by police. That attacker was identified as a 25-year-old Islamic convert from a village near the capital who had become radicalized. Don't want to miss our real-time updates?
